subsection: 2. Conflict in the workplace and its resolution

notes.b: Conflict arises when the interests, expectations or perceptions of employees and employers clash.
points: Pay and conditions: disagreement over wages, bonuses, hours, holidays or pensions is a common source of conflict.
Workload: excessive or unevenly shared work causes frustration among staff and with managers.
Change: new technology, restructuring or new working methods can create fear of job loss and resistance to new routines.
Poor communication: messages that are unclear, late or never sent lead to misunderstanding and rumour.
Personality clashes: differences in working style or temperament can create tension between colleagues.
Discrimination: unfair treatment based on a protected characteristic, such as gender, race or age, creates grievances.
Unclear roles: when responsibilities overlap or are undefined, staff dispute who should do what, or important tasks go undone.

notes.b: Conflict can have positive and negative effects, depending on how it is handled.
points: Positive effect: well-handled disagreement can bring forward new ideas, challenge poor practice and improve decisions.
Absenteeism: unhappy staff may take more sick or unexplained leave, which reduces output.
Low morale: prolonged conflict reduces motivation, commitment and co-operation within teams.
Staff turnover: unresolved disputes can drive talented staff to leave, raising recruitment and training costs.
Industrial action: strikes, work-to-rule or overtime bans halt or slow production and damage customer relationships.
Reputational damage: a public dispute can make customers and potential employees less willing to deal with the firm.

notes.b: Organisations try to resolve conflict inside the workplace before involving outside bodies, and internal approaches are usually faster, cheaper and more private.
points: Grievance procedure: a formal process that lets an employee raise a complaint with the employer, who must investigate it and respond.
Disciplinary procedure: a formal process an employer uses to address poor conduct or performance, with warnings and a chance for the employee to reply.
Negotiation: the parties discuss their positions directly and seek a compromise that both can accept.
Collective bargaining: negotiation between employers and trade unions over pay and conditions for a group of workers.
The shop steward: a trade union representative in the workplace who acts for members and raises their concerns with management.
Human resources: the HR department advises on policy, handles complaints and helps managers deal with disputes fairly.
Internal mediation: a neutral person within the organisation helps the parties communicate and find an agreement.

notes.b: Industrial action is what workers may do when a dispute is not resolved.
points: A strike is a withdrawal of labour, in which workers stop working for a period to pressure the employer.
A work-to-rule means staff do only what their contract strictly requires, slowing work without stopping it.
An overtime ban means staff refuse to work extra hours, which can hold up production or service.
Industrial action is usually a last resort after internal and external procedures have been tried, and Irish law sets conditions on when it is lawful.

notes.b: Conciliation is an external process in which a neutral third party helps both sides reach their own agreement.
points: A conciliator meets both sides, separately and together, to clarify the issues and explore options.
The conciliator helps the sides agree but imposes nothing and issues no recommendation, so any agreement is the parties' own.
Conciliation is voluntary: both sides must agree to take part, and either can withdraw.
In Ireland, conciliation services are provided by the Workplace Relations Commission.

notes.b: Mediation is a voluntary process in which a neutral mediator helps the parties communicate and find common ground.
points: A mediator guides the discussion and helps each side understand the other's position.
Mediation focuses on communication and common ground, and it often preserves working relationships.
It suits disputes between colleagues who must keep working together, where the relationship matters as much as the issue.
Mediation can settle a dispute before a formal grievance or disciplinary hearing becomes necessary.

notes.b: Arbitration is an external process in which a third party hears both sides and makes a decision.
points: An arbitrator hears evidence and arguments from both sides before reaching a decision.
The third party decides the outcome; the parties do not write the settlement themselves.
Arbitration is usually agreed by both sides, and where they agree to it in advance the decision is generally binding on them.
Arbitration is more formal than conciliation or mediation, with hearings and a written decision.

notes.b: Adjudication is a formal decision made by an official body under the law, rather than a settlement reached by the parties.
points: An adjudication officer of the Workplace Relations Commission hears an individual complaint under employment law and issues a decision.
Adjudication does not depend on the parties agreeing to it in advance, because the process is set by law.
Decisions on individual complaints can generally be appealed to the Labour Court.
The Labour Court can also issue recommendations on industrial relations disputes that are referred to it.
External approaches are normally used when internal procedures have failed or the parties cannot agree.

keyTerms.definition: A formal process that lets an employee raise a complaint with their employer, who must investigate it and respond.
A formal process an employer uses to deal with poor conduct or performance, usually with warnings and a chance for the employee to respond.
Negotiation between employers and trade unions over pay and conditions for a group of workers.
A trade union representative in a workplace who represents members and raises their concerns with management.
A process in which a neutral third party helps both sides reach their own agreement, without imposing a settlement.
A voluntary process in which a neutral mediator helps the parties communicate and find common ground to reach an agreement.
A process in which a third party hears both sides of a dispute and makes a decision on it.
A formal process in which an official body, such as a Workplace Relations Commission adjudication officer, hears a complaint and issues a decision under the law.
Action taken by workers, such as a strike, work-to-rule or overtime ban, to pressure an employer during a dispute.

questions.prompt: Explain two causes of conflict in a workplace and the effect each cause could have on the organisation.
questions.model: Unclear roles cause conflict when two employees each believe a task is theirs, or when a task is left undone because nobody accepted it. This can lead to duplicated work and resentment, which lowers morale. Poor communication causes conflict when important changes are announced late or not at all, so staff hear rumours and resist changes they do not understand. This slows the adoption of the change and can lead to formal complaints.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between conciliation and arbitration as external approaches to resolving a workplace dispute.
questions.model: In conciliation, a neutral third party meets both sides, helps them clarify the issues and explore options, but imposes nothing and issues no recommendation, so any agreement is one the parties reach themselves. In arbitration, a third party hears evidence and arguments from both sides and then makes a decision, which the parties are generally bound by when they agreed to arbitration in advance. The key difference is who controls the outcome: in conciliation the parties do, while in arbitration the arbitrator does.

questions.prompt: Analyse how internal procedures could resolve a dispute over workload before it reaches an outside body.
questions.model: A grievance procedure lets the affected employee raise the workload problem formally, so the employer must investigate and respond. This shows staff that complaints are taken seriously and sets a timetable for a solution. Negotiation between the employer and the employee, or with the shop steward if the employee is a union member, allows the parties to compare the workload with the contract and agree adjustments, such as redistributing tasks or bringing in temporary help. Human resources can support this by reviewing workload data, checking role descriptions and advising the manager on fair allocation, which reduces the chance of the dispute recurring. If direct talks stall, internal mediation by a neutral person within the organisation can help the parties communicate and find a compromise before the matter goes to the Workplace Relations Commission.
